//: The assumed safety requirements and element failure modes of
docs/certification/SAFETY-MANUAL.md, each tied to the code that implements
it and the check that demonstrates it.
The manual is an out-of-context safety argument: an integrator reads it and
designs against it. A claim in it that quietly stopped being true would be
worse than no manual, because it would be believed. So every claim names
its evidence here, and tools/common/check/check-safety-requirements.py fails the build
when an id in the manual is missing from this file, when a claim names
evidence that no longer exists, or when the two disagree about which ids
This is the traceability F-14 and F-15 want, at the granularity the safety
argument actually uses. It is not the whole of either finding: 49,401 lines
trace to eight requirements here, and unit-level requirements remain

assumed_safety_requirements.statement: A partition shall not read or write memory belonging to another partition or to the element.
No mapping shall be simultaneously writable and executable.
A partition shall reach a resource only through a capability it holds.
A device shall not access memory outside the region its driver was granted.
assumed_safety_requirements.status: met on x86-64 and AArch64; not provided on ARMv7-A (AoU-6)

assumed_safety_requirements.statement: Memory released by one partition shall not be readable by the next.
On detecting an inconsistent internal state, the element shall enter its safe state rather than continue.
Data supplied by a partition shall be validated before use.
Admission of a real-time workload shall be refused when the set is unschedulable.
assumed_safety_requirements.status: partially met -- no worst-case execution time is claimed (AoU-4)

assumed_safety_requirements.statement: Data the element has stored on a volume shall be returned as it was stored or refused with an error, never returned altered, and what a commit has reported durable shall survive a loss of power.
assumed_safety_requirements.status: met at the btrfs crates' interface, for single-device SINGLE or DUP volumes with CRC-32C, under AoU-15 and AoU-16; accidental alteration only

//unsafe_obligations: Why unsafe exists in the certified item (finding F-26): a closed set,
derived from what the item's unsafe sites do, each tied to the ASR, FM or
AoU above it serves and to the code that argues it. Every unsafe block,
unsafe impl and unsafe fn in the core and item rings names one, as
`// SAFETY: (ID)` or at the head of its `# Safety` section;
tools/common/check/check-unsafe-audit.py resolves the id and holds the untagged

unsafe_obligations.name: Device registers
unsafe_obligations.covers: A load or store to a register window or I/O port of a device the kernel drives itself -- a console, a timer, an interrupt controller, an IOMMU unit, a framebuffer -- mapped as device memory and claimed by the kernel alone.

unsafe_obligations.name: Processor registers
unsafe_obligations.covers: A read or write of the running processor's own state that is neither translation nor protection: interrupt masks, barriers, cache maintenance, idle hints, identification and counter registers, timers, the interrupt controller's CPU interface, debug registers, scratch registers, model-specific registers.

unsafe_obligations.name: Protection and speculation controls
unsafe_obligations.covers: Turning on, or relying on, a processor protection feature: SMEP, SMAP and UMIP, PAN, the user-access window's stac and clac, and the side-channel defences -- speculation-control registers, predictor and buffer flushes, return-stack filling, SSBS.

unsafe_obligations.name: Address translation
unsafe_obligations.covers: Installing or removing a translation root, invalidating TLB entries, dropping the identity map, and reading or writing a page-table descriptor in the frame that holds it.

unsafe_obligations.name: Memory a device reads or writes
unsafe_obligations.covers: IOMMU root, context and stream tables and queues, interrupt translation tables, virtqueue rings and buffers, and a pinned or quarantined frame a device may still write.

unsafe_obligations.name: Frame contents through the direct map
unsafe_obligations.covers: Reading, writing, zeroing or copying a frame of RAM through the kernel's direct map: a memory object's pages, a frame cleared before it is handed out, a copy-on-write copy, a start block or trampoline another processor starts from.

unsafe_obligations.name: A partition's memory
unsafe_obligations.covers: Copying to or from a partition's memory for a system call, through the frame the partition's own tables name, with its address space's lock held (V-01).

unsafe_obligations.name: Execution context
unsafe_obligations.covers: Preparing a kernel stack, switching stacks, saving and restoring a program's registers -- general, floating-point, thread pointer, segment and TLS state -- and entering or resuming user mode, through a signal frame or not.

unsafe_obligations.name: Trap and system-call entry
unsafe_obligations.covers: Installing what the processor enters the kernel through: the GDT, IDT and TSS, the vector base, the system-call registers, the privilege and interrupt stacks.

unsafe_obligations.name: Firmware and platform calls
unsafe_obligations.covers: A call into firmware or the platform: PSCI and SMCCC through hvc or smc -- power, reset, starting a processor, workarounds, the TRNG -- a reset port, the triple fault, the emulator's exit port.

unsafe_obligations.name: What the loader and the image hand over
unsafe_obligations.covers: Reading a structure the loader, the firmware or the image's own assembly placed in memory: the boot information, the ACPI tables and the device tree, the kernel's own text, the vDSO's bytes.

unsafe_obligations.name: Kernel memory ownership
unsafe_obligations.covers: The kernel's own memory: the global allocator and the heap's backing pages, the page array, vmap buffers, kernel stacks and their release, a box taken back from a raw pointer, the loader's memory given back.

unsafe_obligations.name: Shared kernel state
unsafe_obligations.covers: State reached through an UnsafeCell, a raw pointer or a Sync claim whose exclusion or lifetime is argued rather than typed: single-threaded early boot, masked interrupts, a lock taken or released by hand, a processor's own record, a 'static published once, and the interrupt and preemption controls the locks are built on.

unsafe_obligations.name: Deliberate faults in self-checks
unsafe_obligations.covers: An access or a trap a boot self-check makes on purpose to prove a handler or a mapping: a breakpoint, a debug-register trap, a write that must fault and be mapped on demand, an access through an address space under test.
